awd_titl_txt: RAPID: Data Analysis and Modeling of the Grounding Zone of Thwaites Glacier, West Antarctica
awd_abstract_narration:
Global sea levels have fluctuated dramatically in the past and are expected to continue doing so in the future. It is crucial to be able to forecast future global sea level as a significant portion of the world’s population and built environment is located along vulnerable coastlines. The most crucial uncertainty in predicting future sea level rests with the behavior of the great ice sheets, particularly the marine-based Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica. As glaciers melt and calve into the ocean, they contribute to a rise in the global sea level. It is necessary to collect all existing observational data in the ocean surrounding the Thwaites Glacier and to put that data into a mathematical equation, allowing a glacier forecast to be created. This is analogous to a weather forecast typically found on a smartphone. The estimates would provide society with a prediction of the global sea level change over this current century and beyond.

This project will incorporate recently collected observational data in and around the Thwaites Glacier into a computational ocean model with a dynamically static, thermodynamically interactive representation of the ice shelf. This project is a follow-up to the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration project, which focused on observing and modeling the Thwaites Glacier system. There is an urgent need to integrate the collected data into a model, particularly at the grounding zone of the glacier, while the necessary familiarity and expertise to understand the data and incorporate it into a modeling framework are available to the community. This data-model assimilation holds strong promise for delivering a deeper insight into the physical mechanisms that guide the evolution of the Thwaites system and its potential to impact the rise of global sea levels significantly. We will use the MITgcm ocean model to simulate ocean circulation within the ocean cavity beneath the glacier. A high-resolution mesh will enable increased resolution in critical regions, such as the grounding zone and areas with complex coastal geometry. The high-resolution mesh will also accurately represent the geometry of the seaside, seabed, and ice base. The model developed for this project will be the most detailed model ever made of the ocean cavity and potentially represent a significant step forward for modeling ocean–ice interaction in general.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project improved scientific understanding of how ocean waters interact with Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica, one of the world’s most important glaciers for future sea-level rise. Thwaites Glacier is currently losing ice at a rapid rate and contributes significantly to rising global sea levels. Understanding the processes that control its stability is essential for improving predictions of future coastal impacts around the world.

The project successfully combined observational data collected through the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration with advanced computer modeling to study the flow of ocean water beneath the floating ice shelf connected to Thwaites Glacier. Because direct observations beneath Antarctic ice shelves are extremely limited, numerical models are an essential tool for understanding conditions in areas that cannot be easily measured.

A major outcome of the project was the development of a high-resolution computer model capable of simulating ocean circulation and melting beneath the Thwaites Glacier Ice Shelf in unprecedented detail. The model incorporated field observations collected by previous research expeditions and provided new insight into how warm ocean water reaches the glacier and contributes to ice loss. The work improved understanding of the pathways through which heat is transported beneath the ice shelf and identified regions that are especially sensitive to changes in ocean conditions.

The project also advanced knowledge of the factors that influence melting near the glacier’s grounding zone, where the ice sheet begins to float on the ocean. Processes occurring in this region play a critical role in determining the future stability of the glacier and its contribution to sea-level rise. By identifying ocean regions that have the greatest influence on melting, the project provides valuable information that can guide future scientific observations and improve larger-scale climate and ice-sheet models.

In addition to its scientific contributions, the project supported the professional development of an early-career researcher, providing training in advanced numerical modeling, data analysis, scientific communication, and project leadership. The project also created opportunities for mentoring undergraduate students and contributed to broader educational activities within the university community.

The results of this work strengthen the scientific foundation needed to predict future changes in Antarctica and their consequences for global sea levels. Improved understanding of ocean-driven ice loss will help researchers, policymakers, and coastal communities better assess long-term risks associated with climate change. The project contributes to ongoing national and international efforts to improve projections of sea-level rise and to better understand the processes controlling the stability of the Antarctic Ice Sheet.
